title: Recurrent late-onset seizures with worsening memory and age-75 investigation findings
purpose: Interpret seizures, cognition and biomarkers with their measurement context.
decision_point: Reconstructed review of the first comprehensive admission at age 75 (Ex. 1), restricted to clinical observations and sample findings assigned to age 75 or earlier. The published age-75 amyloid concentrations are supplied as retrospective research records, not asserted to have been available to the treating team during that admission.
opening: A 75-year-old man with late-onset focal seizures is admitted for worsening memory and seizures that have become daily. Review the available longitudinal records and the first comprehensive investigation packet.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Integrate seizure burden, treatment history, cognitive trajectory, EEG, imaging and any CSF findings received. Explain what they support and what remains uncertain about the cause of cognitive symptoms. After up to six question turns, give a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. Use only evidence through age 75 and the explicitly retrospective Ex. 1 sample record. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
adaptation: Published age-based clinical observations are paraphrased into a clinician record review. Opening, task, six-turn limit, requirements and release rules are researcher-designed. Routine clinical records are experimentally withheld until requested. The publication reports Aβ samples assayed together after storage, so the age-75 sample values are an explicitly retrospective research packet rather than invented real-time clinical availability. No later clinical outcome or later sample value enters this packet. No precise age-75 cognitive score is read from an unverified figure, and no later medication or autoimmune/amyloid result is moved back to the first admission.
hidden: Age-78, 80, 81, 82 and 84 reassessments; levetiracetam addition, later gabapentin replacement/perampanel and response; subsequent cognitive improvement/relapse; serial later CSF, FDG-PET and amyloid PET findings; later authors' causal hypotheses. Later recovery or biomarker trajectories are not evidence for the age-75 assessment.

facts.text: At age 60, a right-handed man with 16 years of education presented with transient forgetfulness. At 61, episodes involved olfactory hallucinations followed by blank staring and oral automatisms. Routine EEG initially showed no apparent epileptiform activity, but the clinical diagnosis was medial temporal lobe epilepsy.

Carbamazepine was stopped after a drug eruption. Valproate monotherapy, reported at up to 800 mg/day, was associated with seizure remission by age 64. Gabapentin was added at age 74 after recurrent seizures and right frontotemporal sharp waves on repeated EEG; its dose and the exact current valproate dose are not supplied here.

At age 70 he noticed mild memory difficulty: MMSE was 29 and WMS-R Logical Memory II delayed recall was 11/50. Forgetfulness worsened, and delayed recall was 6 at age 74. The narrative reports further worsening by admission at 75 but does not supply an exact age-75 cognitive score in this packet.
Focal impaired-awareness seizures recurred at age 72 after earlier remission, increased by 74 and became daily by the admission at 75 despite treatment.

At 74, brain MRI including susceptibility-weighted sequences showed mild diffuse atrophy without hippocampal sclerosis, microbleeds, amyloid-angiopathy features or significant vascular burden. FDG-PET showed no significant hypometabolism. At 75, repeat MRI and FDG-PET showed no significant interval change. No age-75 amyloid PET result is supplied.

At 75, 24-hour video EEG recorded six clinical seizures with ictal discharges arising in the left frontotemporal region and spreading through the left hemisphere. Table 1 also lists interictal spike/sharp-wave and sharp-transient counts, but explicitly states that sharp transients were not definitively epileptiform.

For the age-75 Ex. 1 sample, the published CSF results are Aβ40 13,671 pg/mL; Aβ42 1,549 pg/mL (reported reference >674); Aβ42/40 ratio 0.113 (reported reference >0.118); and p-tau 74.6 pg/mL (reported reference <50.0). These are the retrospective published sample results; real-time availability of the amyloid values at 75 is not asserted.

The first lumbar puncture was at 75, so pre-epilepsy CSF biomarker levels are unknown. The article states that stored Aβ samples were measured in duplicate in one analytical batch after one freeze-thaw cycle; p-tau was measured during routine practice at each puncture. Timing of cognitive testing relative to recent seizures was not systematically recorded.

reference: At the selected review, integrate recurrent focal seizures, worsening memory, documented delayed-recall decline and active age-75 video-EEG seizures with largely stable structural/FDG imaging. Keep earlier right-frontotemporal EEG findings distinct from the age-75 left-frontotemporal ictal recordings. If the retrospective CSF packet is received, distinguish preserved absolute Aβ42 from a reduced ratio and raised p-tau using the supplied ranges; these do not by themselves establish the predominant cause of cognitive symptoms. Epilepsy-related cognitive effects and coexisting neurodegenerative pathology may both remain plausible. Do not claim reversibility, later amyloid deposition or a medication-caused biomarker change from evidence unavailable at this point. Note missing cognitive-test timing and contemporaneous assay availability. Candidate requests, differential prioritisation and next steps await clinical confirmation.

answer:
Assessment: Age-75 Admission

A 75-year-old right-handed man presents with daily focal impaired-awareness seizures and progressive memory decline. Seizures began at 60 with olfactory hallucinations and oral automatisms, achieved remission on valproate by 64, recurred at 72, and became daily by 75 despite valproate and gabapentin. Delayed recall fell from 11/50 (age 70) to 6/50 (age 74), with further worsening by admission.

Three explanations are considered. First, Alzheimer's disease: the retrospective Ex. 1 CSF sample shows Aβ42 1,549 pg/mL (ref >674), Aβ42/40 ratio 0.113 (ref >0.118), and p-tau 74.6 pg/mL (ref <50), consistent with amyloid and tau pathology, but these values were not available to the treating team. Imaging shows only mild diffuse atrophy without hippocampal sclerosis and no significant FDG-PET hypometabolism, atypical for established AD; no amyloid PET was performed. Second, epilepsy-related cognitive impairment: daily left frontotemporal seizures could contribute to memory symptoms, yet cognitive decline preceded seizure recurrence and no structural lesion was identified. Third, an unresolved lateralisation discrepancy: interictal sharp waves were right frontotemporal (age 74) while ictal discharges arose from the left frontotemporal region (age 75), unexplained and possibly indicating a bilateral or evolving process.

Uncertainties include the absence of an exact age-75 cognitive score, no broader neuropsychological profile, and the retrospective nature of the CSF amyloid and tau values. Proportionate next steps are formal neuropsychological testing, amyloid PET, and further EEG to clarify lateralisation.

scores.name: Factual accuracy and groundedness
scores.reason: The submission is mostly accurate: seizure history, medication course, cognitive scores (MMSE 29, delayed recall 11/50 to 6/50), EEG findings (right frontotemporal sharp waves at 74 vs left frontotemporal ictal onset at 75), imaging (mild diffuse atrophy, no hippocampal sclerosis, stable FDG-PET), and the retrospective CSF values (Aβ42 1,549 pg/mL, ratio 0.113, p-tau 74.6 pg/mL) all match the supplied records, and it correctly flags the CSF results as retrospective. Two minor issues prevent a higher score: (1) it states seizures 'began at 60 with olfactory hallucinations and oral automatisms', whereas the record shows transient forgetfulness at 60 and the ictal features at 61; (2) it asserts 'no amyloid PET was performed', while the environment feedback explicitly says no age-75 amyloid PET result is supplied and nonperformance must not be inferred. Neither error is dangerous or likely to mislead clinical management, so this fits the Score 3 anchor (minor, clinically inconsequential inaccuracies) rather than Score 2 (significant errors or unsupported fabrications).

scores.name: Problem representation
scores.reason: The submission synthesises the available age-75 evidence into a clinically meaningful representation: it integrates the 15-year seizure course (onset at 60, remission on valproate by 64, recurrence at 72, daily by 75), medication history (carbamazepine stopped for drug eruption, valproate, gabapentin added at 74), cognitive trajectory (delayed recall 11/50 at 70 falling to 6/50 at 74 with further worsening), EEG (right frontotemporal interictal sharp waves at 74 vs left frontotemporal ictal onset at 75, preserving the lateralisation distinction as instructed), and imaging (mild diffuse atrophy, no hippocampal sclerosis, no FDG hypometabolism). It correctly treats the Ex. 1 CSF amyloid/tau values as retrospective and not available to the treating team, and appropriately qualifies unresolved gaps (no exact age-75 cognitive score, limited neuropsychological profile). The three prioritised explanations are defensible and provisional. One minor defect prevents a top score: the statement that 'no amyloid PET was performed' slightly overstates the record, which only says no age-75 amyloid PET result is supplied and warns against inferring nonperformance. This is a minor limitation that does not materially misframe the problem, so Score 4 (accurate integration with appropriate qualification, minor limitations) fits better than Score 5, while Score 3 is too low since no consequential gap is inadequately qualified and no defining available feature is omitted or distorted.

scores.name: Differential Diagnosis Generation
scores.reason: The submission gives a clinically plausible differential: Alzheimer's disease supported by the retrospective CSF findings (reduced Aβ42/40 ratio 0.113 vs ref >0.118, p-tau 74.6 vs ref <50) and epilepsy-related cognitive impairment supported by daily left frontotemporal ictal discharges on video EEG. It appropriately flags that cognitive decline preceded seizure recurrence and that imaging was largely stable, and correctly treats the CSF values as retrospective. However, prioritisation and support are incomplete: the third 'explanation' (lateralisation discrepancy) is a finding rather than a diagnosis, so the differential effectively has only two diagnostic candidates, and other important alternatives for progressive amnestic impairment at 75 (e.g., frontotemporal, Lewy body, or vascular contributions) are not considered even as lower-priority items. Discriminating findings are partially used but the ranking between AD and epilepsy-related impairment is left largely unresolved without proportionate weighting of prior plausibility. This matches Score 3: plausible differential with incomplete prioritisation and support from discriminating findings.

scores.name: Trend detection
scores.reason: The submission correctly identifies the direction of both key trends: cognitive decline (delayed recall falling from 11/50 at age 70 to 6/50 at 74, with further worsening by admission) and seizure burden progression (remission by 64, recurrence at 72, daily by 75 despite valproate and gabapentin). It also characterises magnitude where the data permit, citing the actual supplied values from Q2 (12.cognitive_course). Clinically, it interprets the trends appropriately: it links the declining recall to candidate explanations (AD-type pathology versus epilepsy-related impairment), notes that cognitive decline preceded seizure recurrence, and correctly distinguishes the earlier right frontotemporal sharp waves (Q2/Q3) from the age-75 left frontotemporal ictal discharges (12.age75_video_eeg), while flagging stable imaging (12.imaging_through_75). It appropriately handles the retrospective CSF values (12.age75_csf_sample) as not clinically available at the time. No trend direction is stated incorrectly and no clinically important trend is omitted, so this meets the Score 5 anchor.

scores.name: Trajectory interpretation
scores.reason: The submission correctly reconstructs the trajectory: seizure onset at 60, remission on valproate by 64, recurrence at 72, daily seizures by 75 despite valproate plus gabapentin (Q1–Q2), and delayed recall decline from 11/50 (age 70) to 6/50 (age 74) with further worsening by admission (Q2). It grades the evidence appropriately: it keeps the age-74 right frontotemporal interictal sharp waves distinct from the age-75 left frontotemporal ictal discharges (Q3), notes that MRI/FDG-PET were largely stable without hippocampal sclerosis or hypometabolism (Q4), and correctly treats the Ex. 1 CSF amyloid/tau values as retrospective and not available to the treating team, distinguishing preserved absolute Aβ42 from the reduced ratio and raised p-tau. It links the trajectory to management decisions (formal neuropsychological testing, amyloid PET, further EEG for lateralisation) and flags genuine uncertainties (no exact age-75 cognitive score, no broader neuropsych profile, retrospective CSF). This meets the anchor 'Correct, graded, and linked to management decisions'.

scores.name: Context seeking
scores.reason: All three frozen essential requirements were met through targeted, appropriately timed requests. R1 (seizure semiology, burden, treatment history) was requested in Q1; R2 (cognitive trajectory and testing context) in Q1/Q2; R3 (EEG, imaging, CSF) in Q3/Q4, including the deferred imaging group and the retrospective CSF sample with reference limits. Requests were prioritised logically (history → medications/cognition → EEG/imaging → imaging/CSF), matched the two-group cap constraints, and each had a prospectively allowed note explaining the clinical rationale. Unavailable details (exact doses, age-75 cognitive score, timing of testing relative to seizures) were requested adequately and do not count as acquisition failures. No unnecessary requests were made, and the retrospective nature of the amyloid values was respected. This meets the score-5 anchor: essential requirements met with proportionate, discriminating requests and clear task-appropriate explanation.

scores.name: Appropriateness of expressed uncertainty
scores.reason: The submission clearly separates established facts (documented seizure course, delayed-recall decline, video-EEG ictal findings, stable MRI/FDG-PET) from probable and possible explanations (AD pathology supported by retrospective CSF but tempered by atypical imaging; epilepsy-related cognitive effects; an explicitly 'unresolved lateralisation discrepancy'). It names the sources of uncertainty — retrospective CSF availability, absent exact age-75 cognitive score, missing neuropsychological profile — and identifies concrete next steps (formal neuropsychological testing, amyloid PET, further EEG) to reduce them. Confidence is calibrated to evidence strength (e.g., CSF values 'consistent with' rather than proving AD; lateralisation 'possibly indicating' rather than asserting). One minor imprecision ('no amyloid PET was performed' versus 'no result is supplied') slightly weakens calibration, but the overall structure meets the score-5 anchor: distinguishing established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions, explaining uncertainty sources, and specifying the next information needed.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

D3a.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

D3a.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
D3a.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
D3a.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

anchors.1: Misses a clinically important trend or states its direction incorrectly.
anchors.3: Identifies the correct direction but omits magnitude or relevant clinical interpretation.
anchors.5: Correctly identifies direction and, where the data permit, characterises magnitude and clinical significance.
Correct, graded, and linked to management decisions

D5c.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

D5c.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
D5c.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
D5c.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

evaluation_input.answer:
Assessment: Age-75 Admission

A 75-year-old right-handed man presents with daily focal impaired-awareness seizures and progressive memory decline. Seizures began at 60 with olfactory hallucinations and oral automatisms, achieved remission on valproate by 64, recurred at 72, and became daily by 75 despite valproate and gabapentin. Delayed recall fell from 11/50 (age 70) to 6/50 (age 74), with further worsening by admission.

Three explanations are considered. First, Alzheimer's disease: the retrospective Ex. 1 CSF sample shows Aβ42 1,549 pg/mL (ref >674), Aβ42/40 ratio 0.113 (ref >0.118), and p-tau 74.6 pg/mL (ref <50), consistent with amyloid and tau pathology, but these values were not available to the treating team. Imaging shows only mild diffuse atrophy without hippocampal sclerosis and no significant FDG-PET hypometabolism, atypical for established AD; no amyloid PET was performed. Second, epilepsy-related cognitive impairment: daily left frontotemporal seizures could contribute to memory symptoms, yet cognitive decline preceded seizure recurrence and no structural lesion was identified. Third, an unresolved lateralisation discrepancy: interictal sharp waves were right frontotemporal (age 74) while ictal discharges arose from the left frontotemporal region (age 75), unexplained and possibly indicating a bilateral or evolving process.

Uncertainties include the absence of an exact age-75 cognitive score, no broader neuropsychological profile, and the retrospective nature of the CSF amyloid and tau values. Proportionate next steps are formal neuropsychological testing, amyloid PET, and further EEG to clarify lateralisation.
evaluation_input.source: https://doi.org/10.3389/fnagi.2026.1807027; adapted published facts; later outcomes withheld.
evaluation_input.reference: At the selected review, integrate recurrent focal seizures, worsening memory, documented delayed-recall decline and active age-75 video-EEG seizures with largely stable structural/FDG imaging. Keep earlier right-frontotemporal EEG findings distinct from the age-75 left-frontotemporal ictal recordings. If the retrospective CSF packet is received, distinguish preserved absolute Aβ42 from a reduced ratio and raised p-tau using the supplied ranges; these do not by themselves establish the predominant cause of cognitive symptoms. Epilepsy-related cognitive effects and coexisting neurodegenerative pathology may both remain plausible. Do not claim reversibility, later amyloid deposition or a medication-caused biomarker change from evidence unavailable at this point. Note missing cognitive-test timing and contemporaneous assay availability. Candidate requests, differential prioritisation and next steps await clinical confirmation.

requirements.requirement: Request seizure semiology, burden over time and antiseizure treatment/control history.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: Daily seizures and cognitive worsening require assessment of the active epileptic problem and its treatment context before attribution of the cognitive syndrome.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: A targeted epilepsy history or longitudinal neurology-record review covering seizure recurrence/frequency and medicine response/adverse effects. Exact drug names or unreported current doses need not be guessed.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Seek cognitive baseline, change over time and the context of cognitive testing relative to seizures.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: The task asks about worsening memory in recurrent epilepsy; a single cognitive label does not describe its trajectory or establish its cause.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Earlier/current cognition and functional history or serial cognitive records, with a question about recent seizures, testing timing or an equivalent assessment of seizure-related confounding. Missing timing or an absent age-75 score does not count as an acquisition failure after an adequate request.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

requirements.requirement: Request the objective investigation evidence needed for the requested multimodal interpretation.
requirements.presentation_based_rationale: The final task explicitly asks how EEG, imaging and any CSF findings affect attribution, so exact records and test context matter more than assuming a biomarker label.
requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: Review the current/earlier EEG and structural imaging together with any available CSF biomarker values and reference limits, or an equivalent comprehensive age-75 investigation-packet request. A request for an unavailable or withheld amyloid scan still counts, and no later result is required.
requirements.deadline: Before the final assessment, within the six question turns.

interview.decision_point: Reconstructed review of the first comprehensive admission at age 75 (Ex. 1), restricted to clinical observations and sample findings assigned to age 75 or earlier. The published age-75 amyloid concentrations are supplied as retrospective research records, not asserted to have been available to the treating team during that admission.

turns.question: Could you provide the seizure semiology (focal features, duration, frequency progression), the antiseizure medications tried and their responses, and the timeline of cognitive decline (domains affected, rate of progression) from the admission records?
turns.notes: Establishing seizure type, treatment response, and cognitive trajectory is essential to narrow the differential between structural, inflammatory, and neurodegenerative causes of combined seizures and dementia.
turns.feedback: The medication history and responses in 12.medication_history and the cognitive trajectory in 12.cognitive_course are deferred because of the two-group cap, not unavailable. Exact seizure duration is not supplied by these frozen stored groups. No later medication, recovery, biomarker or reassessment result may be moved into the age-75 review; the retrospective Ex. 1 amyloid marker remains applicable if CSF records are requested later.

turns.question: Could you provide the antiseizure medication history (agents, doses, responses, adverse effects) and the cognitive trajectory (domains affected, rate of progression, any formal neuropsychological testing) from the records available through age 75?
turns.notes: Medication response and cognitive trajectory are central to distinguishing progressive neurodegeneration from seizure-related cognitive impairment and to guiding further workup.
turns.feedback: The exact current valproate dose and gabapentin dose, an exact age-75 cognitive score, and a broader detailed neuropsychological domain profile are not supplied in the selected frozen records. This does not establish that other testing was not performed. Use only the documented MMSE/WMS-R and memory-course information rather than inventing a progression rate or further domain deficits. No further directly responsive group is deferred by the two-group cap; later medicines, outcomes and reassessments remain outside the age-75 review.

Gabapentin was added at age 74 after recurrent seizures and right frontotemporal sharp waves on repeated EEG; its dose and the exact current valproate dose are not supplied here.

Forgetfulness worsened, and delayed recall was 6 at age 74. The narrative reports further worsening by admission at 75 but does not supply an exact age-75 cognitive score in this packet.

turns.question: Could you provide the EEG findings (including the right frontotemporal sharp waves and any other epileptiform or non-epileptiform features) and the neuroimaging results (CT or MRI, with any noted atrophy patterns, lesions, or other abnormalities) available through the age-75 admission?
turns.notes: EEG and imaging are essential to distinguish epileptic encephalopathy, structural pathology, and neurodegenerative atrophy as contributors to the cognitive decline.
